theme: Elihu speaks, a better theology, but still insufficient
readingInstruction: Read Job 32:1-34:37. A new character, Elihu, enters the book. Read his speeches carefully and ask yourself two questions: what does he get right, and where does he go wrong?
settingTheScene: Job’s friends have stopped speaking, because “he was righteous in his own eyes” (32:1). Then a young man who has been listening, Elihu, speaks up. He has waited because the others were older, but he has grown angry at both sides: at Job for justifying himself rather than God, and at the three friends for failing to answer. Elihu is not mentioned in the prologue or in God’s closing words, and scholars have long debated what to make of him. He says some true and fine things, and he also makes errors. Read him critically.
observation: Elihu is the son of Barachel the Buzite, and he is angry with Job “because he justified himself rather than God” (32:2).
He says that he waited because the others were older: “I am young in years, and you are aged; therefore I was timid” (32:6).
“It is not the old who are wise, nor the aged who understand what is right” (32:9).
“The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life” (33:4).
He says, “God speaks in one way, and in two, though man does not perceive it” (33:14), including in dreams and in pain.

“If there be for him an angel, a mediator, one of the thousand, to declare to man what is right for him, and he is merciful to him, and says, Deliver him from going down into the pit, I have found a ransom” (33:23-24).
“Far be it from God that he should do wickedness, and from the Almighty that he should do wrong” (34:10).
He says, “Job speaks without knowledge; his words are without insight” (34:35), and that Job “adds rebellion to his sin” (34:37).
interpretation:
Elihu is a puzzling figure. He is the only one of Job’s four counselors who is not rebuked in the epilogue, but he is also never praised. He speaks for six chapters, and then he vanishes. Most readers have found something to admire and something to be wary of in him.

What he gets right is worth noting. He is right that God speaks to people through many means, including suffering. He is right that God is just. He is right that human beings cannot stand on their own righteousness. His speech about the “mediator” and the “ransom” in 33:23-24 is a high point. It echoes the language that Job himself used in 9:33 and 16:19, and it lifts the idea that there is a way for a sinner to be delivered. Some of what he says points in a direction that will be fulfilled in the gospel.

But he also makes a mistake that is perhaps more subtle than the friends’. He sees suffering mainly as discipline. For Elihu, pain is God’s way of warning a person who is heading for the pit. This is sometimes true, but he applies it to Job, whose pain was never meant as a correction. He tells Job that he is adding rebellion to sin, which is a harsh charge for a man who is not guilty of the original sin.

Elihu also speaks with unusual confidence for a young man. “One who is perfect in knowledge is with you” (36:4). He is certain that he has the answer. His speeches are full of “I will” and “I will declare.” There is a pride in him that the rest of the book will not let stand.

His speeches serve a purpose in the book. They bring together the best of what the friends said and push it toward the speech of God. They show how close a person can come to the truth and still miss the point. Then God speaks, and everything changes.
connection: The “mediator” and the “ransom” of 33:23-24 point to Christ, who “gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:5-6) and to whom “the Spirit” bears witness (John 15:26). Hebrews 12:5-11 develops the idea of suffering as discipline for God’s children. 1 Corinthians 8:1 warns that “knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.”
application:
Think about how you respond to a person who is a good deal younger or older than you. Do you listen well?

When you give advice, test it on yourself. Would you want someone to say this to you if you were in the same pain?

Notice the “mediator” in verses 23 and 24, and spend a few minutes thanking Jesus for being the one who found the ransom.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the different ways he speaks to you.
Ask him to keep you listening, not only certain.
Ask him to make you humble with those who suffer.
